sections.heading: Kangra Fort
sections.content: is located in the valley at the confluence of the Banganga and Manjhi rivulets which serve as a natural moat for the fort. Having seven gateways in the fort, Ranjit Singh Darwaza is one with a massive wooden door flanked by fortifications on both sides. Just before the Andheri Darwaza, a path ascends westwards to the wooded plateau where an isolated mehrab (arch) of the non- existent mosque from Jahangirs days is hidden under thick foliage. Nearby, to the south of the mehrab, is a large stone stepwell, called Kapoorsagar, and other structures in ruins. But the most interesting part of the fort is inside the Darshani Darwaza. sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Monument- Kye Gompa
sections.content: Kye Gompa built in the fourteenth century, the largest and oldest repository of Buddhist learning in the Western Himalayas in the Spiti region has the appearance of a hill fort. In summer very few of the Lamas are in residence, the majority living in their own villages till winter when they return within the sacred walls. Some 200 or 300 monks reside in this monastery in winter. The Gompa has a narrow passage and a winding flight of steps that leads to the topmost building around an open courtyard. There at the top on a raised platform is the zimchung, the chamber where the incarnate of the lama resides. The gompa is a three storeyed structure one of which is literally a basement.The basement is used as the store which stores the treasures of the monastery  old weapons and other artifacts. The gompa has a valuable collection of ancient Buddhist texts called Kangyur. They are also kept in the basement area in a separate square vault with walls having beautiful religious murals. The ground floor of the gompa has an oblong room used as the du khang. The walls of this room are also highly painted with beautiful murals with themes from the jataka and other popular stories. To the right side of the du khang is the gonkhang, a refectory and other rooms. The cells of the monks are boxlike chambers all around at the lower levels. The gompa is also well known for its priceless collection of ancient thangkas.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Monument- Tabo Monastery
sections.content: Tabo Monastery is the oldest Buddhist Monastery in Spiti Valley. It is also one of the most important Gompa in the entire Tibetan Buddhist world. This is the place where the present Dalai Lama will retire to from his duties. High mountains surround the gompa. It was found by Rinchen Tsangpo in 996 CE.. He brought in Kashmiri artists to decorate this gompa which is second in merit only to the Tholing Gompa in Tibet. It is popularly known as the Gem of the Himalayas and has a preserve of ancient Buddhist legacy and houses some of the most sacred texts of Tibetan Buddhism. It also houses a priceless collection of manuscripts and thangkas. Among its treasures are historical murals depicting tales from the Buddhist pantheon. The old section has 9 temples, 23 chortens, a chamber for monks and another for nuns. Five halls arranged in a row are enclosed within the gompa walls. The colourful murals of Tabo come very close to the pure Indian style identified with the rockcut Ajanta and Ellora caves. The technique required the surface to be coated with several thin layers of lime and yak skin glue. It was then burnished vigorously to provide the ground. Next it was smoothed and freshened with animal fat and butter. Natural vegetable dyes and powdered stone colours were mixed with dzo milk and yak urine for painting. The early Indian style murals used a combination of reds and yellows with little stress on landscaping. The area around the principal figures was filled with smaller divinities. In contrast, the images of Tabo wear a serene smile and halfshut dreamy eyes showing introspective devotion.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Chamba
sections.content: Chamba stands on a plateau on the bank of Ravi. It blossomed as the ancient capital of the Pahari Kings and was named after King Sahil Varmans daughter Champavati who is considered the patron deity of the place.

sections.heading: Wooden Chhattries of Lakshminarayan Temple
sections.content: Chamba has numerous ancient temples patterned in the style of local hill architecture made from both wood and stone. Most of the temples in the region including Lakshminarayan, Hari Rai Temple, Champavati temple, Vajreshwari Temple, Hari Har Temple etc. were built in the period between the 8th and 10th centuries. The Lakshminarayan temple consists of a Vimana i.e. Shikhara and GarbhGriha with a small antarala. The Temple has a mandapa like structure also. sections.heading: Costumes, Bhuri Singh Museum
sections.content: The Bhuri Singh Museum named after Raja Bhuri Singh, has the family collection of exquisite paintings of Kangra and Basholi schools, as well as the history of Chamba. The museum also displays wood carvings and ancient manuscripts. Apart from the paintings, other items on display are the embroidered Chamba rumaals, coins, hill jewellery and costumes- both traditional and royal, arms and armour, musical instruments and various decorative objects.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Monument- British colonial architecture Shimla
sections.content: Some of the worlds finest examples of British colonial architecture can be seen in Shimla, the capital of Himachal Pradesh, which was once famous as the summer capital during the colonial period. The buildings like former Viceregal Lodge (now the Indian Institute of Advanced Study) made of greystone, the neo Gothic structures of the Gaiety theatre and the former imperial Civil Secretariat (now the Accountant Generals Office) are some of the examples of the British architecture. Built in Gothic style, the Christ Church is the famous landmark on mall of Shimla which was built over a span of 11 years (1846-1857). The beauty of the church is enhanced by the stained glass windows (five in all) for which it is so famed.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Handicrafts
sections.content: The arts and crafts of any region are a reflection of its environment, people and traditions. So it is in Himachal. Weaving, carving, painting, or chiselling  are an intrinsic part of the Himachal life. From the upper reaches of Lahaul and Spiti down to the lowlands of Kangra  life and its shades are woven in, painted on, felt in soulful rhythms or celebrated with joyous abandon, carved in, engraved whether it is in the miniature paintings of Kangra, the thangka of Spiti, or the beautiful shawls of Kullu.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Handicrafts- Wood
sections.content: Availability of wood abundantly in its forests makes it used profusely for architecture in Himachal Pradesh. The pine and deodar, besides walnut, horse chestnut and wild black mulberry are used for woodcraft. Wood carvings on domestic items are quite different from those in temples or houses. Prominent amongst these designs are: nagbela zigzag line that combines the serpentine pattern with three or four petal flowers in each side of the line; doria continuous line of flowers; kutheri phoola multi-sided figure, sometimes enlarged and the pattern lid in a jali to serve as a ventilator.Houses in all over the valleys of Himachal are extensively ornamented with carvings  on doors, windows, balcony panels etc. The craft also translates into wooden idols of gods and goddesses in traditional styles. Utilitarian objects crafted in wood can be often found in Pahari homes  these may include rectangular boxes to store grains or ornaments. The Gaddi households in Chamba and Brahmaur are famous for their attractive wooden utensils. Villages of Kinnaur still use wooden household utensils extensively. Intricately carved wooden spinning wheels are also in use.

sections.heading: Interesting Facts
sections.content: For centuries, wood has been used in Himachal in the construction and ornamentation of temples, homes, idols and so on. The skill is passed on from one generation to the other. The master wood carver of Chamba, Malik Lateef, for example, belongs to a family of traditional carpenters. His father Ali Baksh worked in the courts of the Chamba king and his artifacts are still preserved in the Bhuri Singh Museum in Chamba.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Handicrafts- Wool
sections.content: It is the extreme cold climate of Himachal that necessitated wool weaving. Almost every household in Himachal owns a pit-loom and it is not unusual to find men and women spinning yarn on spindle The best-known woven object is the shawl, ranging from extremely fine pashmina to the coarse desar. Kullu in particular has been famous for its shawls with striking geometrical patterns and vibrant colours  the distinctive feature being stripes running along the edges. Caps of Himachal are of distinctive styles and are different in every part of the state. In Kinnaur, not only shawls, but also saris, trousers and pyjamas are woven in wool. The shawls woven in Rampur, known as Rampur chaddar, are famous for their soft texture and durability. In Chamba district, the weaving assumes a chequered pattern. Besides shawls, carpets and blankets are an essential part of the Himachal lifestyle. Carpets in brilliant colours are woven with a variety of traditional motifs  there are garudas on flowering trees, dragons, swastikas, flutes symbolising happiness or lotus blooms signifying purity. Carpets are woven as furnishing, as saddles for horses and as blankets or chutkas. They are also a part of every brides trousseau.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Handicrafts- Stone
sections.content: The Shivalik hills have large resources of fine sandstone, which is highly suited for carving, and has played a vital role in keeping alive the stone carvers craft. Numerous stone temples still dot the Himachal landscape. Kangra, Mandi, Bilaspur, Sirmaur, Chamba and Kullu have been traditional centres for stone carving. The giant monolithic carving of the rock cut temple at Masrur in Kangra has been compared to the Mahabalipuram temples for its daring and detailed, elaborate and delicate chiselling.

sections.heading: Vajreshwari Devi Temple, Kangra
sections.content: Objects are crafted with metal for religious, ritualistic and everyday needs of the people of Himachal. There are fine examples of freestanding metal statues at temple entrances in Brahmaur, Chamba and the Vajreshwari Devi temples in Kangra. Repousse technique was used to create beautiful temple doors. Low settees made of silver or brass are another common ritual artifact used in homes as well as temples, besides bells, incense burners, lamps, jars, flasks, tridents, fly whisks, and canopies. Brass is often used in the hills for fashioning household utensils. The Kinnaur metalsmiths also specialise in the repousse worked door handles fashioned in the form of crocodile, dragon or lion-head. All sacred buildings display these handles. Another interesting item is the dongbo or tea churner, as common as the intricately carved hookah bases.

sections.heading: Jewellery
sections.content: in Himachal is artistic, elaborate in style and is inspired from nature itself. The designs reflect nature in simple motifs like seeds, flowers and leaves being developed into exquisite patterns. Different communities wear jewellery unique to their traditions, but some ornaments are worn all over the state, which include the hemispherical shaped chak  worn on the forehead and both sides of the head, neck ornaments like hansli or small pendants called toke, chandanhaar - a necklace comprising five or seven rows of facetted gold beads. The choker worn here is called kach and consists of silver beads and triangular plaques. Chiri tikka is a flat piece of silver, enamelled or embedded with pearls and suspended from the centre of the forehead while several chains hang along the hairline on both sides. A heavy bunch of silver tassels or flowers, attached to the plait with a smaller ornament is tied to the plait ends. Men, women and children often wear silver amulets to ward off evil spirits. Sunarion ki Gaon near Rohru is a village, where many families are engaged in jewellery designing and crafting.

sections.heading: Rumaal , V&A Museum Collection
sections.content: The big handkerchiefs called rumals of Chamba are famous and have always been a symbol of love and a good omen. They are presented at festivals and weddings. They are also used for wrapping ceremonious gifts exchanged between the bride and bridegrooms families during marriages. These rumals are embroidered very attractively. The designs show clear influence of miniature paintings. It is done in running stitch without any gaps in between and space filled so that the same figure appears on both sides of the cloth. Rasamandal, hunting, Nayika Bhed, Shiva family and Mahabharata are popular themes embroidered on the rumal.

sections.heading: Interesting Facts
sections.content: Historically, the craft mainly flourished during the reign of Raja Umed Singh of Chamba (1748-68). The oldest rumal dates back to the 16th century and is said to have been embroidered by Bebe Nanki, sister of Guru Nanak. This piece is now kept in the Sikh shrine in Hoshiarpur. Another important rumal was presented by Raja Gopal Singh to the British in 1883 and is now displayed at the Victoria Albert Museum, London. This piece depicts the battle of Kurukshetra.

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Fairs & Festivals- Minjar
sections.content: Himachal Pradesh is not only a place of charming landscapes and mystifying woods but also of colourful festivals with fairs and dances as its integral part. Minjar is one of the most important harvest festivals of Himachal, which is celebrated for seven days. This is a kind of a thanksgiving ceremony to the God of rain and a prayer for good harvest. Processions with decorated horses and banners are taken out through the streets to mark the beginning of the fair. In keeping with tradition, all the gods and goddesses are brought out in colourful palanquins on the banks of the river

sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Fairs & Festival- Dushehra
sections.content: Himachal Dushehra is a week-long celebration which takes place with great fervour in Kullu. From the little temples in the hills, deities are brought in procession to the maidan, to pay homage to the reigning deity, Raghunathji. sections.heading: Himachal Pradesh- Fairs & Festival- Sui Mela, Pathroru, Lishoo
sections.content: Other important fairs and festivals including Sui Mela, Pathroru and Lishoo are celebrated in this region. Held for 15 days in the month of Chaitra (March-April), Sui Mela is a fair to commemorate Sui Mata, a beloved deity of the region. Women gather to sing, dance and worship the Devi during this festival. The event is an all-women affair  men are strictly prohibited from participating in the mela. Pathroru is a month-long festival of fire and flowers, which is celebrated in Chamba with much fervour. The chira (a structure of wood and earth to which dry grass and flowers are tied) is worshipped in the belief that it will destroy pests that come with the rains. It is also known as Prithvi puja (or earth worship). Baisakhi is known as Lishoo, which is an agrarian festival celebrated differently in different regions of Himachal.

sections.heading: Dangi Dance
sections.content: The Dangi of Chamba, Gee dance of Sirmaur, Naati of Kullu, are all a part of their festivities. The vast repertoire of pahari folklore often gets translated into these songs. These ballads dwell on village romances, chivalry and the changing seasons. The songs are

sections.heading: Interesting Facts
sections.content: The Paharis are partial to a whole lot of musical instruments without which pahari music wouldnt be half as interesting. The kangarange is the most commonly used stringed instrument. Among the wind instruments are the bhopal, shamal, bugial, and shehnai (different kinds of pipes), the damentu (horn), the highly ornate narsingha (hornpipe) and the sanai (hautboy). To keep the rhythm of the various dances percussion instruments like the damane, anga, dhol and dholak (drums), the hulki (an hourglass-shaped drum), the kartal (clappers), khanjiri (tambourine) and jhanja (large cymbals) are played.
